Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good day and welcome to the Earnings Conference 
Call of Craftsman Automation Limited. 
 
As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode. There will be 
an opportunity for you to ask questions after the opening remarks are 
concluded. Should you require any assistance during the conference call, 
please signal an operator by pressing “*” followed by “0” on your touchtone 
telephone. 
 
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Srinivasan Ravi – Chairman and 
Managing Director of Craftsman Automation Ltd. Thank you and over to you 
sir. 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Good afternoon, everybody and thank you very much for joining the Earnings 
Call for today. 
 
I just want to touch upon briefly on the last two quarters and about the 
opportunity for Craftsman as well as the headwinds we had with the war as 
well as the commodity prices which was spiking very sharply and now it is on 
a lower trajectory. So, we weathered all these situations, we have put up a lot 
of capacity, still capacity is getting created as we speak, not all capacities have 
come into production and some of the pipelines are not full yet. We are on a 
growth path and we will be continuing this growth path into H2 as well as in the 
next two financial years. Some of the orders what we are doing is some are 
short-term, medium-term prospects and also long-term prospects. The long-
term prospects, the CAPEX has been done bulk in the stationary engine side 
which you all are aware. The revenues will start from FY'29 and go into FY'30 
where we will peak at around $100 million and the next level of peak we are 
expecting in the enquiries and order push is quite strong. 
 
Aluminum is having a strong headwind and we are adding more capacities 
across our plants and our subsidiaries also. The DR Axion Plant-2 has started 
at least trial production I would say and the order book is also strong there. 
Sunbeam has gone through a very good transformation and we are in close 
contact with the customers on the way forward. Q3 and Q4 will be looking 
better for Sunbeam and next financial year I think we will be also getting new 
orders from new customers while we are leveraging the capacities for newer 
products which will give better benefits. And also across all customers and all 
product lines especially the legacy products, we are in contact with customers 
for the price rationalization or price reset in cases of legacy products and this 
has to be done for almost all suppliers is what we feel because of the sharp 
rise in manpower cost, energy cost and all other associated costs. The capital 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 2 of 13 
 
goods cost has been steadily rising I mean that any new projects cannot be 
done at old prices so we are also very careful. 
 
One good thing about Craftsman is we have been continuously doing CAPEX 
and bulk of the CAPEX has been even before the big rise in the capital goods 
cost has increased. Now capital goods also it is not easy to put up CAPEX 
because of the long gestation period. There is a huge bottleneck for supply of 
capital goods across the world so we are in a strong position to win more orders 
and also we are winning more orders as we speak. We are little more selective 
on the customers as well as the product looking at the lifecycle and profitability 
since we have now the base which is stronger and our ability to attract slightly 
larger customers with more profitable products for supply within India or 
outside India is better now on the position because of our bigger size. 
 
The growth in Powertrain is expected to continue and also strong growth in 
Aluminum. Yes, we have seen some corrections of the margins in Aluminum 
that is not a correction, it is a temporary correction. We had increased our 
inventory because of the shortage of raw material and also the prices which 
were increasing dropped suddenly so we had an impact of that. So, with the 
price increase what we are negotiating with the customer or correction or 
compensation for the Aluminum price correction also which will play out in the 
coming two quarters. I think most of the customers are open to that discussion. 
We will see the benefits coming into the next two quarters. 
 
Now, I will leave the floor open for any Q&A. 
 
Moderator: 
Thank you very much. We will now begin the question-and-answer session.  
Please note that some of the statements made during this earnings conference 
call may constitute forward-looking statements which are subject to risks and 
uncertainties and are not guarantees of future performance. We encourage 
you to refer to the disclaimer section in the company's investor presentation. 
Further, the management will not be addressing any customer-specific queries 
due to confidentiality obligations. Participants are requested to avoid 
mentioning customer names while asking questions. 
 
The first next question is from the line of Chandramouli Muthiah from Goldman 
Sachs. Please go ahead. 
 
Chandramouli Muthiah: My first question is just around the gross profit line. I think that's an easier line 
for you to manage growth on. First half growth has been at about 30% YOY on 
gross profit. 2Q has also been around that range. So, just related to a lot of the 
business that you've been winning and the capacity that you've been adding, I 
just want to understand over the next 12 months to 18 months when you expect 
the inflection in gross profit growth, just related to all this capacity that's coming 
on board and business that's being won? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Thank you for the question. I would say that this sort of growth will continue if 
you look at an year-on-year basis for quite the next two quarters, three 
quarters. We are quite confident about the growth because of the past 
investments and past developments of the products and the pipeline which is 
already there, products being approved or plants coming on stream. Other than 
the headwinds what we had on the energy cost, mainly the gas and also the 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 3 of 13 
 
Aluminum spike which has let a little ripple in this quarter, last quarter. 
Otherwise, we feel that overall growth will continue in all the segments in the 
Powertrain, not all segments of the Powertrain. Of course, tractor we will see 
some contraction in the next two quarters. Apart from that on the powertrain 
we'll see growth. So, overall growth on the powertrain is we are quite confident 
about that. Similarly, on the Aluminum, the pipeline is quite long for the 
whatever order wins we have. There are some headwinds on the new plants 
where we have to put in the working capital in and we have to start up the 
plants which is also happening as a suboptimum as of now. So, the operating 
leverage on those plants will take another two quarters to get into a profitable 
situation, more profitable situation. So, this is dragging down a little, but this is 
temporary I would say. But whereas the mature plants are having an 
advantage on the operating leverage. But as I said earlier, bulk of the margins 
also will come from the price correction which has to happen across almost all 
the OEMs. 
 
Chandramouli Muthiah: Got it. That's helpful. Just to follow up on the price correction, roughly what 
magnitude do you think you need to take price spikes for the factors you 
mentioned; manpower, energy costs and so on? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
See it depends from customer to customer, product to product also and the 
time when the first order was placed. If the orders were placed in the last few 
quarters, I don't think that is feasible for any customer to give. But there are 
legacy products which are not corrected and also the volume has contracted 
on some of the legacy products where it is a drag. Yes, it requires a big reset I 
would say in that case. And in certain cases, yes, it is more on manpower and 
power and other regular inflation which is related. It may vary, but anywhere 
between 6%-7% all the way to 15%-20% will be there depending on the 
commodity, the product and the time of the order. This is not on the top line, 
but on the gross margin or the value addition portion. It might not impact too 
much on the OEMs there on the top line, I would say, as far as we are 
concerned. The top line may be with the commodity prices; we cannot really 
put a number to it of what is the percentage there. 
 
Chandramouli Muthiah: Got it. That's helpful. And my second question is just around, there's been 
recent news flow around one of the large domestic passenger vehicle 
manufacturers and then their partnership now expanding with all the global 
passenger vehicle manufacturers. So, I just want to understand, there are 
some news reports that there might be a local engine of the local passenger 
vehicle maker becoming an expanded scope in the global platform in this 
partnership. So, I just want to understand your thoughts on how that situation 
is evolving and what the opportunity size could be for a company like 
Craftsman? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Not only the customer, the OEM you are talking about, what I can guess it is 
across all the OEMs present in India who are multinational and also Indian 
OEMs. Whatever product is suitable in India for the Indian passenger vehicle 
consumer, those products are very competitive and these are the same 
products which are required in some of the underdeveloped markets or even 
South American, African markets and some parts of Asia. So, logically, India 
will become a manufacturing hub, if not for the vehicles themselves, but at least 
for the Powertrain, which is logical. The second thing is there is a proof here 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 4 of 13 
 
on tractor, on the small tractors up to say 120 horsepower. India has become 
a global power for tractor manufacturing and all the OEMs across the world 
have invested into India for capacities for export out of India also. So, the same 
trend also seen on the two-wheeler side that exports of two-wheeler from India 
is increasing. Also on the construction equipment, not on the high-end 
construction equipment, but on the construction equipment where we have 
bulk requirement India, we see exports also happening. So, exports out of India 
as a product or an aggregate will continue to grow. So, there is opportunity for 
all tier 1, tier 2 suppliers like craftsman for on the growth strategy. 
 
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Senthil Kumar from Joindre 
Capital Services. Please go ahead. 
 
Senthil Kumar: 
Just wanted to know about the gross debt. The gross debt increased from Rs. 
3,340 crores in March 2026 to Rs. 3,618 crores in September 2026 
consolidated figure. This is despite the debt repayment using QIP proceeds. 
Could you elaborate what is the reason for this increase? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
The net debt is only around Rs. 3,000 crores because we have got a lot of cash 
available and some capital advances which we have paid. Our top line growth 
is quite significant. So, working capital has ballooned and also the other say 
GST credit has ballooned and some of the pipeline we have added more lines 
or more plants. So, that pipeline inventory is yet to materialize into revenue on 
the matter. So, yes, and we are also carrying some safety stock of material 
which now will get diluted in the coming quarter. So, overall the CAPEX, we 
have done significant CAPEX in the first half. So, overall I think we will be at 
1.7-1.8 net debt to EBITDA on a consolidated basis for the year. And I 
mentioned that the inflection point for us is around Rs. 1,850 crores sort of 
EBITDA which we will reach next year. After that we will be able to be self-
sufficient for funding our CAPEX as well as the maintenance CAPEX. So, we 
have done a big surge of CAPEX to cater to a larger customer base and the 
end segment base. So, this one time we have pivoted that we want to keep the 
growth path, we have committed a 15% CAGR. Of course, some years we will 
grow much more than that. In the real terms not adjusted for inflation is what 
we say that we will be growing at 15%. Our base is quite strong, I mean large. 
So, considering all that I think this is, we have taken land for putting new plants. 
The land is partially utilized but that land will serve for the next 3, 4, 5 years for 
our expansion. And infrastructure also has been, basic infrastructure has been 
put. So, additional equipment will not take too much CAPEX. So, this is like 
building a new airport. I think we have taken this decision to expand our 
footprint in manufacturing. 
 
Senthil Kumar: 
What would be the gross debt level by end of FY'27, given this challenging 
environment? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
I would rather say it will be 1.7x-1.8x net debt to EBITDA overall on a 
consolidated level. I do not want to give a forward-looking statement on 
EBITDA but you know the EBITDA you can reverse calculate it for H1 and 
definitely H2 revenue will be more and H2 normally the EBITDA also is better. 
So, I would leave it at that.

Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Vignesh from SIMA Wealth. 
Please go ahead. 
 
Vignesh: 
Just want to understand on the medium-term outlook, are we looking for any 
other new segments entering into it apart from heavy HP engines? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Practically, no new segment but we are vigorously expanding the powertrain 
capacity, the Aluminum casting capacity and machining capacity and we have 
done bulk of it. So, we expect that to yield results in the coming quarters in a 
better way. Otherwise, we are also broad basing on the new product on the 
Aluminum components, not only the legacy parts but I think there are more 
opportunities coming in not only on the EV but in general, the product offerings 
of the OEMs have become more wider. So, we are seeing opportunities there. 
 
Vignesh: 
Okay sir, and regarding the second phase of this high engines or how is it 
coming out? Like what are the revenue targets we are planning? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
So, as we speak, we are getting inquiries for the next level of capacities. Most 
of it is on the same products, what we are already developing that is welcome 
that means gestation period to market will be improved. We are discussing that 
to add some capacities there. Second thing is we are looking at broad basing 
the value-added subject that hereafter we are trying to build up facilities which 
are little more flexible in nature to cater to various customers looking at the 
global market outlook. So, all this will be more attractive for the customer to 
reach out to us to get their product quickly developed or quickly ramped up. 
So, I would not like to reveal that how much inquiries we received but I think it 
is still going strong. Today AI I think is here to stay and the backup power 
generators or the mainstream generators required for that will continue to grow 
over the next 5-7 years. 
 
Vignesh: 
So, tentatively as the first phase reaches a peak revenue in FY'30, once that 
is done we will start the second phase, we can assume like that? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Yes, you can assume like that and second phase will not be capital intensive 
because our infrastructure is already in place for the foundry as well as the 
fundamental machine shop. So, there after that it becomes interesting that 
incremental CAPEX and the incremental revenue growth will be more 
attractive. 
 
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Joseph George from IIFL. 
Please go ahead. 
 
Joseph George: 
Thank you. I had a couple of topics to discuss. One was on cash flows. So, this 
year you have raised Rs. 2,000 crores of QIP and if I look at the run rate of 
CAPEX in the first half of the year which is about Rs. 1,100 crores plus there 
is a lot of cash drain on working capital. Considering all of that how do you see 
the net debt position at the end of FY'27 compared to FY'26 end? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
So, I said today that one thing is that our growth on absolute terms has been 
say 50% but I would discount that with the commodity side. But on an overall 
base if you look at it as a standalone, the real terms itself we have grown 35% 
on a larger base. That means our capacities are much more than that in total.

So, this means the capex and the working capital cycle is yet to play on the 
number of days which we will see more. In the Q4 the exit rate will give a very 
clear indication of what are the things to come in next year. So, we are in the 
build-up stage now. So, I don't think this is giving a right picture about what is 
happening at our end. 
 
Joseph George: 
Okay, sir. Fair enough. And in terms of capex for the full year should we expect 
a similar kind of run rate in 2H as we have seen in 1H? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
No, I think we are quite clear about Q3 to a decent extent. But Q4 we might not 
do much CAPEX for the simple reason that our other CAPEX are little more 
long-term and that will be pushed into subsequent years in a phased manner. 
It will not be coming as big as this because we have broken the one level where 
we have put up greenfield facilities across India, I would say, on both the 
powertrain and Aluminum segments. To answer your question, Q3 on a 
console level will be between Rs. 500 crores-Rs. 600 crore on the CAPEX. 
 
Joseph George: 
Okay, understood. The second question or topic I wanted to chat on was the 
Sunbeam business. So, I remember about a couple of quarters back, you had 
mentioned that you will give up on low margin business, low margin revenue 
and improve the mix and get to early teens or mid-teens kind of a margin, 
maybe in a year or two. I want to understand where we stand on that journey. 
Have you started giving up low margin businesses or what's the path from 
here? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Yes, our customers request us to support until the festive season, which we 
have done for this festive season. So, those products will go away in the next 
couple of months. Handing over is happening where they're developing 
alternate or whatever maybe. So, overall, the exit of certain smaller customers 
is mostly complete, but the bigger customers we are handholding. So, our top 
line may reduce, but our absolute margins will improve because some of them 
are negative on the EBITDA itself in general. There's no point in trying to reset 
those prices. So, with that, the P&L will be very healthy. 
 
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Sagar Shetty from Wealthyvia. 
Please go ahead. 
 
Sagar Shetty: 
My question was regarding first of all that we have recorded a good top line 
growth and at the same time, we have seen that the margins were a bit 
declining. So, is it right to assume that we have seen some sort of Aluminum 
pass through during this quarter? So, if you could just throw some light on that 
and why was the margin a bit lagging? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Yes, the Aluminum, some of it we are still in discussion with the customer for 
the corrections on the matter. Until we come to a conclusion, we cannot book 
the differences, number one. Number two is the steep rise and there is a panic 
in the market of the availability of material itself. Added to that is the Middle 
East crisis. See, we wanted to protect our customer product lines. So, we had 
to take an extreme step of ordering more, not knowing which material will be 
supplied or which material will not be supplied. So, we have gone a little 
overboard, but I think that will stand us in the long run. Even to be frank with 
you, some of the customers asked us to give the Aluminum to them for them 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 7 of 13 
 
to give to other suppliers. That was the situation. So, for that, we have taken 
some brunt that when the prices dropped, yes, we have some impact. There 
is a one-time impact, but it does not go into impact on the longer term. Yes, on 
Q2 especially, yes. And in Q3, there will be very marginal and Q4, there will be 
nothing there. 
 
Sagar Shetty: 
Okay. And my next question was around when I view at the Q2, there was a 
new German subsidiary. So, if we just throw some light on it, like what is the 
purpose and investment planned in it? And at the same time, if you would also, 
like what is the growth rate in German subsidiaries as of now? Like what is the 
quarter run rate which we should expect going forward? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
So, I will just explain the German subsidiary, even though it looks a number of 
companies. Fundamentally, there is one holding company, which is holding a 
real estate company and then the holding company is holding a foundry, that 
is it. The foundry is the only manufacturing company as of now. And that 
company is quite, I think it has reported a healthy growth in the revenue and 
also the profitability is very decent. And this is also supplying to large engine 
family products and which is sustainable going forward. And all the expenses 
are indexed with the customer. In the case of power, all the raw materials and 
also the labor cost. So, we do not see any risk on the business and it is a 
steady business and it is profitable. Coming to what is the new company which 
we have done, only the formation has been done there. The machining portion 
is now outsourced to some smaller companies in Germany. Since our growth 
is big, we thought Craftsman, yes, we have capability in machining. So, we 
want to take a small, put a small machine shop there, which will help our 
customers to give more orders to us there. So, in this case, we have not 
decided the quantum of investment. It will be very small. You know that we 
have invested around Rs. 100 crores to Rs. 130 crores, something like this, in 
the German subsidiary. But machine shop will be a small, a very small 
percentage when compared to that. 
 
Sagar Shetty: 
Yes, please. So, I just wanted to know, are we planning any future CAPEX like 
in the foreign subsidiaries going forward? Like apart from the Rs. 1,500 crores 
outlay which we had, anything extra for the foreign subsidiaries going? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
No, foreign subsidiary, no. As I mentioned, it will be nothing. The subsidiary is 
a small machine shop. So, what we are thinking through is only very small, 
maybe 20, 30 crores on a couple of machines there, so that we can support 
the foundry and reduce the working capital intent, because now we are 
sourcing the machining outside and there is a delay. We will continue to 
outsource the machining with other machine shops there. But the incremental 
requirement, we may do it inside. This is only an optional subject. It is not any 
CAPEX intensive business what we are doing. I want to make one very clear 
statement is, we are not a fan of investing outside India in a big way because 
we understand the risks which are associated. This is a very strategic 
investment and we will keep it in that way. 
 
Sagar Shetty: 
So, just adding one question. Does this also rule out a possibility of foreign 
acquisition? 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 8 of 13 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Yes, if you look at our history, we are always very averse for many, many 
decades. We see what is the life cycle left in this sort of businesses which is 
coming for acquisition. So, we believe that any company coming up for sale, 
the good companies will get merged with the bigger brothers there in Europe 
itself. There are other companies there. So, we feel that we stand more 
exposed or be more risky for us unless there is a technological advantage or it 
is very small when compared to the parent. Look at our size of revenue outside 
India. It is almost 4% top line of German subsidy. 4% of our revenue is coming 
from our subsidiary and if you look at the gross net block of the investment 
also, it may be hardly 2%-3%. 
 
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Akshay Karwa from Aviva 
India. Please go ahead. 
 
Akshay Karwa: 
My first question pertains to the stationary engine segment for data centers. In 
the opening remarks, you noted that the current order book is around $100 
million. On that, when do we expect to book revenues within this and what 
could be a target by FY'29 and approximately your monthly run rate for this 
stationary engine segment? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
FY'30, we will reach the run rate at least by Q3 or Q4 for that $100 million. 30% 
by FY'28 is what we feel, 50% by FY'29. 
 
Akshay Karwa: 
Okay. Thank you, sir. Lastly, on the margin guidance, if you look at this quarter, 
Aluminum segment has seen a margin decline of almost to 6.5% EBIT margin. 
You mentioned that you will talk with customers. What do you see here for the 
closing margin for FY'27 and FY'28? If you can touch upon that. Just on the 
margin guidance for the Aluminum segment for FY'27 and FY'28? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
It will go back to the normal after our discussions with customer happens. Yes, 
we are still in discussion with the customer. Some are for the past impacts that 
you have taken and some are for the future corrections. Both will be discussed, 
finalized. It will not be only for Craftsman. It will be for the entire Aluminum 
supplier community and also the OEMs. OEMs are also aware of this. A lot of 
dialogues are happening. Beyond that, because of the sensitivity of the 
information, I cannot share. 
 
Akshay Karwa: 
Also, the nominal run rate of around 12%-13% for Aluminum segment? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Again, the commodity price has gone up. We have to equate the same 
commodity price, then the margins should come back to normal after the 
discussions with the customer. But commodity price is a subject where we 
cannot get the increased Aluminum price, we cannot get a margin for that 
Aluminum also. So, we have to look at it that way. Some moderation will be 
there. 
 
Akshay Karwa: 
I understood, sir. That's all from me. I wish you all the best. 
 
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Chirag Jain from Emkay 
Global. Please go ahead.

Chirag Jain: 
Yes, good afternoon, sir. Post GST cut, we have seen very strong growth for 
the entire auto industries. This year also, growth seems to be surprising. What 
are your thoughts for the overall auto industry growth probably next one or two 
years and particularly the 15% growth guidance that you gave? How much that 
is dependent on the underlying automotive industry and how much would be 
more driven by bottom-up order wins that we have done across various 
customers and platforms? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
We have not factored too much auto growth, but I feel that auto growth will 
continue in a way quite a strong way, especially on the passenger vehicles as 
well as two-wheelers because of the inflection point of per capita GDP. Also, 
the value per product is also increasing because of the two-wheelers. I think 
the 150 cc and above also is going to grow in the near future, which will give 
more opportunities for us. Similarly, also on the passenger vehicle, newer 
models with newer prices and there will be realignment on the supplier base. 
We will get more opportunities. We will have a combination of new products 
replacing old products and we will be a supplier for the new products. That is 
one advantage. Second thing is exports out of India is also continuously 
increasing. The third thing is value. For example, if a hybrid vehicle comes in, 
there will be more transmission parts which are available. If BS-7 comes in, 
then the new engines also will come in. All this gives an opportunity for us. The 
last but not least will be the in-house manufacturing to outsourcing. The trend 
in the future will increase for outsourcing. Many of the OEMs are still 
manufacturing a lot of Aluminum components in-house, but we see the trend 
slightly starting to shift now. 
 
Chirag Jain: 
At this point of time, any sense how much will be in-house and how much will 
be outsourced from an OEM perspective on the Aluminum side? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
The major market player, I think most of it is insourced, the key parts totally. 
The second largest player, also quite a big percentage is inside their company. 
I don't want to make names here. For two-wheelers also, it is the same trend. 
There are somebody who is totally outsourcing, almost totally outsourcing. 
Some are still almost totally in-house, at least on the machining side, on the 
two-wheeler side. And two-wheelers, some of the people are still making the 
castings also, so without getting their names. 
 
Chirag Jain: 
And what is driving the shift towards more outsourcing? 
 
Srinivasan Ravi: 
Earlier, the capability of suppliers were not there, number one. So, they had to
